No. 20· 29 October 2026· Global, Italy in focus· Illustrated edition
In three lines

  1. Omnicom calls its IPG integration "substantially completed" and immediately wins Coca-Cola's North America media account, the same week Salesforce agrees to pay $5.66 billion for Braze, two more pieces of the marketing pipeline folding into fewer, bigger hands.

  2. McDonald's is ending a 32-year FIFA World Cup sponsorship after its "biggest-ever" 2026 campaign underperformed, betting on its own IP instead, exactly as Walmart and Sephora bet their holiday campaigns on borrowing someone else's beloved character.

  3. The two biggest new TikTok sounds this week, JADE's "Angel of My Dreams" and Tate McRae's "Housewife," both trace back to the same single live event: the Victoria's Secret Fashion Show on October 18.

The world

marketingdive.com · October 23, 2026

Omnicom says its IPG takeover is "substantially completed," then wins Coca-Cola's North America media

Omnicom CEO John Wren told investors the integration of Interpublic Group, closed nearly a year ago in the largest-ever agency acquisition, is "substantially completed." The combined group posted $6 billion in Q3 revenue (7.2% organic growth year on year, 5.8% for the first nine months), with the integrated media segment growing over 10%, and is on track for its planned $900 million in cost savings this year. The same quarter, Coca-Cola handed Omnicom its US and Canada media account, worth an estimated $785 million a year starting December 1. The win comes weeks after Omnicom lost PepsiCo's global media business, handled for decades, to Publicis (this brief's issue 5). Omnicom also won Novo Nordisk's US media buying in the quarter and manages $9.9 billion in sports sponsorships group-wide.

Why it mattersThe same holding company lost one soda giant's media account and won the other's inside two months. When the whole industry consolidates into two or three holding companies, a client leaving one of them has fewer places left to go, and the accounts that do move are worth hundreds of millions of dollars each.
ppc.land / SEC filing · October 20, 2026

Salesforce agrees to pay $5.66 billion for Braze

Salesforce signed a definitive agreement to acquire the real-time customer engagement platform Braze for $47.50 a share in cash, about 27% below Braze's 2021 IPO price. Braze, which coordinates personalized messages across apps, email, SMS and WhatsApp for roughly 2,770 customers (349 of them paying $500,000+ a year), grew revenue 24% to $738.2 million in its last fiscal year. Salesforce plans to fold Braze's real-time engagement and AI decisioning into its Agentforce and Customer 360 products; the deal is expected to close in Salesforce's fiscal 2028, which starts in February 2027. Braze CEO Bill Magnuson said the product will "continue building as Braze."

Why it mattersAnother marketing-technology category, real-time customer messaging, stops being a standalone market and becomes a feature of one of four or five giant platforms. The pattern is the same as Omnicom-IPG: fewer owners controlling more of the pipe a brand's message has to travel through.
adweek.com · October 23, 2026

McDonald's ends a 32-year FIFA World Cup sponsorship after its biggest campaign underperformed

McDonald's is walking away from its FIFA World Cup sponsorship after more than three decades. The split follows this summer's World Cup campaign, built by Wieden+Kennedy New York and run in more than 110 countries, which McDonald's called its largest marketing push of 2026. CFO Ian Borden told investors on the Q2 earnings call it "provided a lift to the business and generated excellent system excitement" but ultimately "underperformed versus our expectations," with US sales growth slowing over the same period. The move is part of a wider shift toward developing and promoting McDonald's own intellectual property rather than renting a third party's platform.

Why it mattersMcDonald's biggest-ever sponsorship push, in the biggest sports event on earth, still wasn't enough to hit its own numbers, so the company is choosing to own a smaller stage outright over renting a bigger one. That is the exact opposite bet Walmart and Sephora are making this week with their holiday campaigns, below.

Campaigns & brand moves

marketingdive.com / adweek.com · October 26, 2026

Walmart recreates The Muppet Christmas Carol to sell its own holiday platform

Walmart and Disney's The Muppets Studio launched "A Who Knew Carol," a full retelling of the 1992 film with Walton Goggins as Ebenezer Scrooge opposite Kermit the Frog, Miss Piggy, Gonzo, Rizzo and Pepe, plus Stephanie Beatriz as Scrooge's niece. It's the latest chapter of Walmart's "Who Knew?" platform, which the retailer has been using to reposition itself as more style-forward to higher-income shoppers. In Walmart's version, Scrooge is visited by three new ghosts: the Ghost of Christmas Presents, the Ghost of Deals to Come and the Ghost of Christmas Fast, each mapped to a different part of Walmart's holiday pitch: gifts, Black Friday savings, fast delivery. CMO William White called it a way to show Walmart can "surprise customers" throughout the season.

Why it mattersWalmart isn't commissioning an original holiday story, it is licensing one of the most beloved Christmas properties in American culture and bending its plot points to match a retail calendar. The emotional investment the audience already has in the Muppets does the persuasion work a new jingle would have to build from zero.
adweek.com · October 26, 2026

Sephora brings in Seth Rogen to be bad at gift shopping on purpose

Sephora's new US and Canada holiday campaign, "We All Sephora," stars Seth Rogen on a mission to find gifts with help from the retailer's beauty advisors. The hero spot, from agency Gut New York and directed by Jason Woliner, shows Rogen leaving the store with a setting spray for his producer, a scent for his cousin and a red-light therapy mask for his mom (and himself). Sephora teased the campaign by rebranding its The Grove LA store to "Sethphora" over the weekend. The campaign rolls out October 29, the same date as this issue, across CTV, linear TV, streaming and social.

Why it mattersThe joke only works because Rogen's own public persona, stoner-comedian energy with no claim to beauty expertise, is the opposite of a beauty-brand spokesperson. Sephora is renting his credibility gap, not his credibility, to make "anyone can gift beauty" land as a punchline instead of a tagline.
spotandweb.it · October 26, 2026 (on air from October 25)

Planted brings plant-based meat to Italian television for the first time

Swiss plant-based meat brand Planted launched its first national Italian campaign, "Approved by Meat Lovers," on Mediaset networks and radio starting October 25, introducing planted.macinato (mince) and planted.spezzatino (stew cuts) to Italian kitchens. The campaign leans on authenticity and irony rather than sustainability messaging, positioning the products as a credible choice for people who still want traditional meat flavors. Agency and media budget were not disclosed in the source.

Why it mattersPlant-based meat brands have spent years selling to people already convinced; addressing the campaign directly to "meat lovers" on mainstream Mediaset reach, rather than niche channels, is a bet that the category's next growth has to come from people who were never looking for a substitute.

What is working in content

Traackr, 2026 State of Holiday Season Report · published July 28, 2026

Holiday creator content is getting more crowded and less rewarding per post, except for brands with existing relationships

Traackr's report, built specifically to forecast this holiday season from 770,000+ creators and 12 million+ pieces of content in the US market, found that "deal content" (discount codes, promo posts) grew 2.5x year on year in volume while the attention each individual post earns fell 63%, and boosted post volume more than tripled. The brands that came out ahead weren't the ones spending the most: the top performers earned 57% of their holiday attention from creators they already had standing relationships with, against 51% for the rest of the market. The report also flagged TikTok Shop and ShopMy gaining attention share while LTK and Amazon's creator programs lose ground, without giving exact percentages for that shift.

Why it mattersThe same logic running through this issue's campaigns, borrow equity instead of building it from scratch, applies to creator budgets too. Dumping more discount content into a crowded Q4 feed is getting less efficient every year; a creator relationship built months earlier is the cheaper way to buy attention in November.

Social trends

Nylon / inmusicblog.com / tixel.com · week of October 18-26, 2026

One live fashion show just gave TikTok its two biggest new sounds of the season

  • JADE's 2024 single "Angel of My Dreams" surged after Kylie Jenner's surprise runway debut, wearing the show's $50 million Fantasy Bra and feathered wings, walking to the track: the audio passed 270,000 TikTok creations, with more than 120,000 of those arriving in just the first two days, and US Spotify streams for the song jumped 2,049% (Nylon, inmusicblog.com).
  • Tate McRae's new single "Housewife," released October 15 and given its live debut at the same show, has driven more than 309,000 TikTok creations as creators apply the song's "domestic fantasy, money and independence" theme to their own lives (inmusicblog.com, tixel.com).
Why it mattersTwo different labels, two different artists, one single live broadcast, and TikTok is still the place both songs actually go viral, not the show's own livestream. The feed remains the real distribution channel for a cultural moment, even when the moment itself happened live on YouTube, Instagram and TikTok simultaneously.

The historical bridge

New York, January 3, 1863

A cartoonist invented Santa's modern image for free. Brands have been renting it ever since.

Thomas Nast drew "Santa Claus in Camp" for the cover of Harper's Weekly on January 3, 1863, in the middle of the US Civil War: a plump, bearded Santa in Union colors handing out gifts to the troops. It wasn't a commission for any company, it was a morale illustration for a political magazine, but over the following two decades Nast kept drawing Santa for Harper's, standardizing the sleigh, the workshop, the red suit and the big belly that most of the world now pictures automatically. Coca-Cola's own illustrator, Haddon Sundblom, built his famous 1931 Santa directly on Nast's template, and nearly every retailer's holiday Santa since has done the same. The character the whole industry leans on every December was never owned by anyone; he was drawn for free, by an illustrator with no product to sell, and has been borrowed by commerce ever since.

Why it still holds. Walmart didn't invent a new holiday mascot this year, it licensed the Muppets. Sephora didn't build a new spokesperson, it rented Seth Rogen's existing public persona. McDonald's, by contrast, just walked away from thirty-two years of renting FIFA's platform to build something it can actually own. A hundred and sixty-three years after a magazine cartoon created the character everyone borrows at Christmas, the same two choices, rent the emotion or build your own, are still the only two options on the table.
